Wikipedia GeoSearch, 3 km radius around Trade and Tryon Streets
Category:Buildings and structures in Charlotte, North Carolina

stops.name: Old Settlers' Cemetery
stops.description: Charlotte's first municipal burial ground, holding graves from 1776 to 1884 including city founder Thomas Polk, great-uncle of President James K. Polk.

stops.name: Fourth Ward Park
stops.description: Three acres of walking paths and fountains that anchor the restored Victorian streets of Charlotte's Fourth Ward.

stops.name: Overcarsh House
stops.description: A Queen Anne frame house with a conical-roofed corner tower, built for Methodist minister Elias Overcarsh and kept in his family until 1966.

stops.name: Liddell-McNinch House
stops.description: An 1890s Queen Anne home once owned by Charlotte mayor Samuel McNinch, who hosted President William Howard Taft here in 1909.

stops.name: First Presbyterian Church
stops.description: An 1857 Gothic Revival church whose spire was rebuilt in the 1880s and whose churchyard sits a block from the towers of Uptown.

stops.name: Charles R. Jonas Federal Building
stops.description: Charlotte's 1915 post office and federal courthouse, later named for the long-serving North Carolina congressman Charles R. Jonas.

stops.name: Discovery Place Science
stops.description: A science museum open since 1981, home to the largest IMAX Dome theater in the Carolinas.

stops.name: Carolina Theatre
stops.description: A 1927 silent picture palace that sat dark for nearly fifty years after closing in 1978 and finally reopened in March 2025.

stops.name: Latta Arcade
stops.description: A 1914 indoor shopping arcade whose glass skylight was built to let cotton buyers grade their crop by daylight.

stops.name: Bechtler Museum of Modern Art
stops.description: Mario Botta designed this museum for the Bechtler family's collection of mid-century modern art, and it opened in 2010.

stops.name: Harvey B. Gantt Center for African-American Arts + Culture
stops.description: A center for African American arts named for Harvey Gantt, Charlotte's first Black mayor and the first Black student admitted to Clemson.

stops.name: Romare Bearden Park
stops.description: A park whose gardens and terraces were laid out to echo the collages of Charlotte-born artist Romare Bearden.

stops.name: Bank of America Stadium
stops.description: Home of the Carolina Panthers since 1996 and of Charlotte FC, seating just over 75,000 at the western edge of Uptown.

stops.name: Mecklenburg Investment Company Building
stops.description: Built in 1922 by Black investors for Black professionals, it is one of the few structures left standing from the razed Brooklyn neighborhood.

stops.name: Grace A.M.E. Zion Church
stops.description: A 1902 Gothic Revival church with two crenellated entry towers of unequal height, among the oldest surviving African American churches in the city.

stops.name: NASCAR Hall of Fame
stops.address: 400 E Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
stops.description: Opened in 2010, it honors the drivers, owners and crew chiefs of stock car racing in the sport's commercial home city.

note: Charlotte has never had a run, so it wins the rotation outright. All sixteen stops sit inside Uptown and form roughly a one mile loop: Fourth Ward north of Trade, down Tryon through the Levine Center for the Arts, then east to Brevard Street and the Second Ward. Every ZIP was looked up against the verified street address and every one came back 28202. Dropped after reading the article: Barringer Hotel (demolished November 2023), Independence Building (imploded 1981), Hotel Charlotte and Merchants and Farmers National Bank Building (both demolished, still carried as NRHP rows), Thomas Polk Park (the article describes it in the past tense, so its current state is unclear). Levine Museum of the New South was left out because the article does not settle whether it still occupies its Uptown building. The Mint Museum was left out because it has one shared article covering two sites and the coordinates point at the Randolph location, not the Uptown one. Charlotte Fire Station No. 4 and the Thomas Trotter Building were dropped for the opposite reason: an NRHP address but almost no article to write an honest sentence from.
